items.question: How do you see the model's ability to interpret genetic variants of unknown significance?
items.object: Interpreting genetic variants of unknown significance with a computational model
items.answer: One of the things that the field of computational biology is often asking is: if you have a genetic mutation in your genome, if I sequenced you, whether that's via 23andMe or some other genetic test, you'll find mutations in your genome. How do we actually interpret those and understand what the functional consequences are? Sometimes you'll get a rare genetic disease. Those are causal genetic mutations that are known to cause a devastating disorder that might be muscular dystrophy or cystic fibrosis or breast cancer, right? But most of the mutations that you have, there's sort of this—we call them variants of unknown significance, which is fancy scientist for “what the hell is going on?” And it turns out the model has an opinion about those mutations and what the hell is going on with them. It turns out it's sort of state of the art in doing that.

items.question: What do you see as the real bottleneck in turning AI-designed drug molecules into medicines?
items.object: Testing and regulatory approval as bottlenecks in AI drug development
items.answer: Well, here's the thing. Even if we had perfect drug design molecules coming out of these pipelines and fancy models, you can design a trillion molecules, 10 trillion, but you still have to actually test them, initially in animals and then in people. That's the real bottleneck. Even if you pack the top of the funnel with all the things, it just takes years to actually go through the regulatory apparatus. I think there are a few intermediate checkpoints along the way in order to realize this potential.

items.question: How do you think evolution can serve as a unifying theory for building biological models?
items.object: Evolution as a unifying theory for biology
items.answer: One of the things that motivates me academically is the idea that we actually have a unifying theory for biology, right? Unlike the physicists who have been scrimping and poking for one for a century, we have this in biology, and it's so obvious that we find it an obvious force: evolution. It acts on biology across all of its different length scales, from entire planets—biology can, for example, terraform planets—all the way down to ecosystems and populations, individuals, our tissues, individual cells, and individual molecules. So that's this unifying force that is actually very deep and rich, and you can learn a lot from it. How do we activate that unifying theory? How do we put it to work? We've been thinking about this in the lab and recently have been training a series of models that we call EVO, inspired by these forces of evolution, that tries to connect biological sequences using this modern sequence modeling paradigm directly to biological function, with the idea that evolution passes down its effects of natural selection throughout generations of life via DNA mutations.

items.question: Why do you see whole genomes as a compelling basis for biological models?
items.object: Training biological models on genomes
items.answer: Last year, multiple Nobel prizes were awarded for AI and for AI in biology, in particular for protein design and for predicting the structure of proteins, to David Baker and to Demis Sabis and John Jumper. If you read those citations, they both explicitly state “for proteins.” We love proteins. These are some of the most important fundamental molecular machines. But our realization, for me as a genome biologist, is that proteins are encoded in DNA along with RNA and regulatory DNA and all of the things that you need to make life. So we asked: could we train a model on genomes with a long-context model so that it could reason over all the different bases and molecules that are embedded inside of genomes to learn about the molecular interactions and how they lead to biological function?

items.question: How do you judge the value of biological AI models when researchers compete over whose model is more foundational?
items.object: Claims of foundational status in biological AI models
items.answer: Predicting the effects of breast cancer-causing mutations: it's best in class at doing this. Or being able to design new CRISPR gene-editing systems. In addition to its zero-shot capabilities, people are building really an app store for biology on top of all of these foundational layers. One of the funny things in modeling today is how everyone's model has to be more foundational than someone else's model. There's a bit of a pissing contest happening. Maybe our model is more foundational than the other models because your DNA versus protein—I mean, and below that there are these all-atom diffusion models, so maybe those are even more fundamental. I don't really know. I think what matters are the capabilities and doing something that actually feels useful. Those are just some examples of what we thought was cool and useful from the model.

items.question: How do you understand EVO’s ability to learn useful biology from next-base prediction?
items.object: EVO’s ability to learn biological patterns through next-base prediction
items.answer:
I can just maybe talk about what the model is. It's an autoregressive, sort of multiconvolutional hybrid model, but you can think of it like a really efficient long-context model that's trained, at least in this version, autoregressively. Basically it does this next-token or next-base prediction, and it turns out, just like in natural language or in vision or in robotics and embodied intelligence, this general machine-learning paradigm is able to find higher-order patterns. Just like if you're doing next-word prediction, you can learn about grammar, color, and world navigation, you seem to learn some rich set of representations about biology by predicting the next base or the next amino acid residue or the next gene. The model learns something about the molecular logic that gives rise to a cell.

It turns out it's sort of state of the art in doing that.

items.question: How do you think about designing AI evaluations that demonstrate meaningful biological understanding?
items.object: Evaluations that demonstrate meaningful biological understanding in AI models
items.answer: When you develop a new type of model, you have to create a lot of the evals as well. That was something that we put tremendous effort into. You see this horizontally across AI in many different domains: folks will build things to the benchmarks. No one really likes building benchmarks. It's gory, requires a lot of taste, takes a lot of time, and you have to continually update them as the models get better. We dealt with a very similar challenge here, which was making evals that would be similar to the AGI or intelligence evals, where it actually feels meaningful when you're able to do it, like Amy or Putin problems or things like that. What would be the equivalent of demonstrating true biological understanding that a cell biologist would feel emotion if you were actually able to solve that? What would it look like to make all molecular biologists feel what the NLP people felt a few years ago?

items.question: How do you think predicting biological sequences lets your EVO models learn from the experiment of evolution?
items.object: The EVO models’ use of evolutionary genomic variation as training data
items.answer: The experiment that's already been done, if you will, is the experiment of evolution. There are different mutations that are what make us different from each other. That's human genomic variation, but also the mutations that make us different from chimpanzees or from worms or from bacteria. The model can just look across this trillions-of-tokens-large dataset and learn those patterns. That was the insight of this EVO series of models that we've been training at ARC: to ask if you could predict that next base, that might be the difference between being healthy or having a sickle cell anemia mutation. Or it could predict the next amino acid residue, and that could be the difference between having a catalytically active binding pocket for a key enzyme in your body physiology or that being a null mutation where that thing doesn't work anymore. Or it could also be the next gene, a gene that completes some biosynthetic pathway, or a different gene that's been removed by some transposon or jumping gene mobile genetic element that's excised it, some sort of viral interference.

items.question: How do you think about the sequence-to-structure-to-function framework in protein language modeling?
items.object: The sequence-to-structure-to-function framework in protein language modeling
items.answer: Structure is another way to have an abstraction of function. You have concepts of convergent evolution, for example, where something has similar function but different sequences and slightly different structures that act out the activity or function of that protein. And so this sequence-to-structure-to-function token or mapping of protein language modeling, I think, is very beautiful. It takes advantage of the central dogma of molecular biology, AlphaFold series. Well, it takes advantage of just our supervised textbook understanding of how biology works. The interesting oxymoron with these models for me is the way that we use them is, just like using ChatGPT, it's text in, text out. EVO is DNA in, DNA out.

items.question: What do you think makes a biological tool widely useful?
items.object: Adoption of biological tools
items.answer: First of all, tools become useful when they meaningfully lower the energy barrier of adoption. It's a catalysis-type activity where everyone uses BLAST for sequence alignment, everyone uses AlphaFold to look at protein structure, everyone uses CRISPR to do gene editing, everyone does NGS to read DNA or RNA.

items.question: How do you envision the role of AI models and agents across the scientific method?
items.object: AI models and agents for the scientific method

items.question: What role do you think Arc Institute should play in advancing biological research?
items.object: Arc Institute’s role in biological research
items.answer: We started the institute to be able to have this mothership that is able to attack long-term research capability breakthroughs and to have the long-term thinking and multidisciplinary expertise in order to actually execute on those goals. I think if you look in biology, one of the interesting things is that a lot of the biggest mechanistic or basic-science breakthroughs do happen in a university context. I would say that's interestingly in contrast to what happens in AI or CS in general.

items.question: How do you understand the differences between academic and industrial biology research today?
items.object: The relationship between academic and industrial biology research
items.answer:
Thirty years ago, the questions that basic science was interested in and industry was interested in were quite different. Today they seem to heavily overlap. There are some things that folks don't typically do in a university lab, like study PK or tox or CMC, or hardcore drug-manufacturing-type things. But folks are interested in molecular glues, induced proximity and degraders, and new drug concepts. Folks are also interested in new machine-learning models, new delivery mechanisms, inflammation and stress, and all kinds of things like this. There's much more heavy overlap.

The type of product that selects what you do upstream is very different. They're structurally different. At the end of the day, you have to optimize for grant funding and first- or co-first-author papers in the academic setting, whereas you do have to make a drug and have dozens to hundreds of people lying behind a molecule or a program to reach the holy land. I think that does lead to differences in strategy. Personally, I think people really overemphasize what's academia and what's industry. The reality is these are heavily overlapping distributions today in how people operate. The differences are a little overblown, but they do have fundamentally different incentives that drive different behaviors. Blending our academic side of the house with our technical-staff side of the house, which is built much more like you'd see in industry, has been part of what we hope will make ARC a model that others want to copy or replicate or propagate.

items.question: How do you approach bringing different disciplines together at Arc Institute?
items.object: Arc Institute’s approach to bringing different disciplines together
items.answer:
We've thought about this deeply at ARC as a convening center, not just between the three flagship research universities here in the Bay Area—Stanford, Berkeley, and UCSF—but also between basic science and the biotech industry, and biology and the technology sector. Our CTO, Dave Burke, just started a few months ago and has really been leading the computational modeling of virtual cells, where we're trying to simulate human biology with these AI foundation models. Dave used to—he actually has a PhD in biomedical engineering from many moons ago—but most recently ran engineering at Android and Pixel.

I think we have also built an entire operational side of the house, from finance to legal to lab ops to facilities to university relations and academic affairs. We run our own space around administration, our own ops, and we try to do much of that like a tech company. We've also recruited on the ops side of the house many people who maybe ordinarily wouldn't work in a basic science or discovery setting, but are motivated by the mission to take fundamental breakthroughs and have a product sensibility where we can get these out into the real world. We're not optimizing at ARC for Nature and Science papers. If you give Berkeley or Stanford professors millions of dollars to do more science, that's almost the default expectation and output. What we really care about are things that could be tangible.

items.question: How do you think about what counts as success for Arc Institute?
items.object: Success and scientific productivity at Arc Institute
items.answer: I think there are lots of ways that you can parse scientific productivity. Journal publications are an important and fundamental part of sharing work with the community and peer reviewing it, but technical blogs, code repos, and protocols are platforms that people can use. I think we want to make technologies and platform capabilities that are broadly useful to create new mechanistic insights, but also actually try to cure some diseases. Over time, if we can be an Edison shop that's inventing or finding lots of cool things, hopefully there'll be real-world value in those things, and there are lots of partners who specialize in this.

items.question: Where do you see opportunities for AI models to improve the pharmaceutical process?
items.object: AI models for improving individual steps in pharmaceutical work
items.answer: Happy to talk about this in the pharma context, which is large, decentralized, sprawling bureaucracies, much like universities or Congress or the SF city governments. Some parts are incredibly functional, and everyone would agree in these different organizations some parts are less efficient. The first thing that hopefully we can see is models that can improve efficiency in discrete individual steps. Can we have a more efficient process for target ID? For molecule design, absolutely making a better binder, and then figuring out the drug properties of those different molecules: selectivity, pharmacokinetics, half-life, expression, manufacturability, what have you. There will be models or model-guided approaches for each of those steps.

items.question: How do you interpret where pharmaceutical companies are finding value in AI today?
items.object: Enterprise AI adoption and the distinction between drug discovery and drug development
items.answer: If you look at how AI is being used today in pharma companies, a lot of them are taking massive regulatory documents, summarizing them, and using AI to help them write more of them. This compression and decompression of information in a structured fashion has been leading to enterprise adoption in this setting. I don't know, I think that says something about the process of where people find things useful. If you talk to some pharma execs—not the drug-discovery organizational leaders, but the budget people who hold the enterprise purse strings—they'll say, “I don't spend actually that much money on drug discovery. I spend most of my money on drug development, so tell me something about drug development. How can AI help me with that?” I think that is a very deep comment, because it says something about where money is spent and where value can be found. The first thing to realize is our industry probability of success is like 10%. A lot of the things that people talk about or complain about or comment on in drug discovery and development falls out of that fundamental statistic.

items.question: What do you think published biology papers leave out about how scientific discovery actually happens?
items.object: The gap between published biology papers and the actual experimental process
items.answer:
I think here's the thing that I find kind of interesting: we have done a lot of biology with what is not that far from guess and check. If you look at what happens in the wet lab, the actual experiments that are happening, you're just kind of in the arena trying, trying out random hypotheses and seeing what happens. The missing reasoning trace in the scientific literature is you don't know what didn't work. Everything is narrativized and written in a story of inexorable logic and vision leading to scientific breakthrough. But everyone who makes the sausage knows that's not what actually happens most of the time.

If you actually work with the research folks at the bench—and this is the case across all technical industries—that high-fidelity reasoning trace of the true process is not written down anywhere. That would be very useful for these reasoning models and for closing the loop and doing multi-agent frameworks.

items.question: How do you think models with predictive power would change biology as a discipline?
items.object: Predictive models and biology's experimental culture
items.answer: If you actually look at what happens, it's guess and check. A model with even a modicum of predictive value would be transformative, though we don't have that. Biology is a very pragmatic, salt-of-the-earth experimental discipline. You see this in the culture of peer review: “Show me the data.” You can't pontificate in your discussion section because you haven't shown any of this stuff. If you read old papers, they were so clear and visionary and high-fluting in a way that papers today aren't. We have this culture that is very pragmatic. Having models that have predictive power will obviously be useful for accelerating the efficiency of science. I think it will also change the culture.

items.question: How do you think predictive models could change the drug-discovery process?
items.object: Predictive models in drug discovery
items.answer:
Well, these are imperfect models. We set up this set of filters in the drug-discovery process where first show it works in cell lines, then show it works in primary cells or in an organoid, then show it works in a mouse, then show it works in a monkey, then test it in people. By the time you've gotten there, five years and a hundred million dollars has gone by. That's very challenging, and that's where I think predictive models will really help. The reason why we do all of these steps in linear series is because we don't have predictive power, so we have to do things in the arena and you have to do it in real life. Growing cells and growing animals takes months to years to actually do those experiments.

The promise of having a predictive model isn't just predictive power. It's that you could actually simulate things in a multi-parallelized fashion. That's the whole idea behind parts of Machines of Loving Grace, which I thought Dario really did get right: if you had something that could be a trusted oracle, you could just run 10,000 agents at the same time.

items.question: How do you see AI agents progressing toward a fully closed-loop scientific discovery process?
items.object: AI agents across the scientific method
items.answer: I think we will see more examples of this coming out over time. Today folks building AI agents for things are basically trying to close the gap between step X and step X plus one, or X plus four, or whatever. Businesses are trying to find the most commercially valuable set of steps, a set size that's as small as possible in step number, in order to make a company. I think we will have agents or copilots at each step in the scientific method, from hypothesis generation to experimentation to data analysis, and the ability to close the loop and write the paper or make the discovery and then decide what to do next is quite far away. Something that's very efficient at traversing the steps, I think, will really take off.

items.question: What did building ARC's virtual cell atlas teach you about the value of AI agents in research?
items.object: ARC's virtual cell atlas and the agent used to build it
items.answer: One of the things that we recently released at ARC is our virtual cell atlas, the world's largest dataset of single cells, that we're using for training these cellular foundation models. The way that it happened was we created an agent that was essentially like a crawler, kind of like a search crawler, but it's able to crawl the Sequence Read Archive and then process the highly unstructured and messy metadata and reanalyze and systematically reprocess all single-cell data. This is running on a cloud bucket instance, just cranking away in a tireless fashion. It's the kind of stuff that a talented computational biologist wouldn't want to do because it's so grindset, but the scale at which we're able to reach is community-wide. That was the leverage and efficiency that our team of really two lead researchers could achieve with one agent. I think that was a huge mental unlock for me. We want to be at the frontier of actually deploying these and making breakthroughs. The meta aspect that folks are going after right now will shake out over time, but I care about using these to actually make breakthroughs as opposed to chart the end-to-end closed-loop path.

items.question: How do you think about programming physiology as a direction for Arc Institute’s biology research?
items.object: Arc Institute’s research on multisystem interactions and programming physiology
items.answer:
I'm tremendously excited about lots of things. The thing that maybe many people don't know is the degree to which we have really been trying to build biology out at ARC. People have maybe heard about our gene-editing work or our machine-learning work, but a lot of what we're actually trying to build is this general concept of applying high-throughput scalable technologies in the context of multisystems interactions, really working at the neuroimmune interface.

We hired two incredible scientists out of Penn last year who study the process of interoception. Proprioception is when you close your eyes and know where your limbs are, and interoception is the idea of “I feel the weather in my knee” or “my tummy feels funny,” midwives' tales type stuff that actually has really deep science. It's totally unknown: how does your body talk to your brain and vice versa? It turns out there's a deep mechanistic basis for this. When people think about programming biology, they think about it in the drug paradigm: how do I get a binder that binds to this protein or how do I get a CRISPR to edit this gene? But if you think about what happens with hormones or with AMPC, you're able to program the way that you think and feel and behave in really powerful ways that control not just satiety but energy, mood, muscle synthesis, focus, all kinds of things. How do we actually program physiology? That's something that I've been spending a lot of time thinking about in our lab.

items.question: How do you think the gut–brain circuits involved in runner's high and stress could change the way we use drugs?
items.object: Gut–brain circuits as a new paradigm for using drugs
items.answer: When you delete these bacteria, you cut off this ENS-to-brain circuit, or you cut off the ability of the brain to release the dopamine. At each of these steps individually, you can block the runner's high. It really traces, in an intact animal—well, this is a mouse study—this full-body circuit. But that also goes in reverse. When you have deep psychological stress, that can lead to signaling from the brain to astrocytes that innervate your gut, that releases pro-inflammatory cytokines, that leads to gut inflammation, and then can give you ulcers. Stress causes ulcers. We've actually kind of known this, but this is the mechanism. How can you treat it? There are folks who get recurring ulcers, and there's a brain-to-body axis by which this signals. I think this happens all the time, some of which is conscious, most of which is unconscious, and you can actually start to figure out the dials and knobs. That's actually, in a way, a new paradigm for drugs, or how to think about using drugs. It's not just this highly reductive pharmaceutical binder-to-biomarker type of thing, but that's giving you more of the holistic, almost Eastern medicine flavor of just how do I feel healthier?

Just like you have your CGM that monitors your glucose with high temporal resolution, you have your Oura Ring or your Whoop that talks about your various biomarkers, or you can go to Quest or Function Health or whatever and get blood tests that measure what's going on with your liver function or your cholesterol or your testosterone or estrogen or other types of hormones. items.question: How do you assess 23andMe's contribution to consumer genetics?

items.answer: I think if you look at 23andMe, it recently filed Chapter 11. I think it's an amazing pioneer and visionary pioneering effort in how to take genetics and put it in the hands of millions of people.

items.question: What would you like to see in a service that combines genetic information with body measurements to guide your health?
items.object: Longitudinal personalized health recommendations
items.answer: The thing that I would really love to see in the world is something that can take all of that information with all of your different body measurements and then connect that to diet and sleep and give you personalized recommendations about your health in a longitudinal way. We have very fragmented datasets for being able to do this today. Being able to collect this data at scale across populations and over time with temporal resolution—I don't want to be one of these unhinged “big data will solve everything” people, but it will.

items.question: What do you hope AI antibody design will enable by the end of 2025?
items.object: AI design of full IgG antibodies
items.answer: My hope is by the end of the year—and this is already happening—we can design full IgG antibodies, not single-chain binders like nanobodies, but the real antibody medicines that we know and love today. We can just design their CDR regions; they're going to bind really well. You can one-shot it and do point and click on that surface of your enzyme: I can just bind it, one chat.

items.question: Why do you see virtual-cell models as an important direction for AI in biology by 2030?
items.object: Virtual-cell models and a cell-level equivalent of the Protein Data Bank
items.answer: I think the thing that will mature over the next couple years is that we can actually design enzymes de novo. That will be really interesting. Again, this is all in the world of proteins, and most people who think about this stuff are very protein-coded. A lot of our work is to zoom out from proteins and think about cells. Building the PDB of virtual cells is something that we've been focusing a lot on at ARC, and that will take some years from today to mature. PDB is a protein data bank, the gold-standard database of experimentally solved protein structures at atomic resolution that was used by DeepMind to train AlphaFold. It's the pretraining data that allows the model to reach some capability like protein structure prediction at angstrom resolution. What is that for virtual cells, which we think would help us design better drug targets and increase therapeutic probability of success? I think that will be my 2030 prediction: accurate and useful virtual-cell models that make cell biologists feel emotion.

items.question: What would you like scientific superintelligence to look like by 2050?
items.object: Scientific superintelligence
items.answer: The 2050 idea—and hopefully this happens much sooner—is scientific superintelligence, or the end-to-end recursion of the scientific method. I'd like to see that with lab in the loop, with a fully automated wet lab that's vertically integrated.

items.question: How do you think predictive models could accelerate drug discovery?
items.object: Predictive models for accelerating drug discovery
items.answer: The only way that I can imagine you speeding this up is if you have a model with strong predictive power. A lot of this hinges on our ability to make models that can actually do that. And I think you will unlock different step sizes of capability based on how good they are.

items.question: How do you think the choice of experimental data could limit predictive models in biology?
items.object: The choice of experimental data for predictive models in biology
items.answer: Basically, if we make the wrong data, I would say, is one obvious one. You can model the mouse in all of its glory to great perfection. It still will not be the human. That's one trivial example of something that we still do, though, because that's just what's practical. I have this other soapbox about how we actually just need to be doing way more experiments in humans.

items.question: What do you think it will take to enable more experiments in humans?
items.object: Enabling more experiments in humans
items.answer: I think there will be some aspect of creativity involved in addition to better regulatory innovation. One example would be you can take samples from brain-dead patients, for example, and then you can get lungs that you can perfuse and keep alive for a week and do experiments in that lung. There was a paper recently published about this.

items.object: OpenAI Deep Research

items.question: How do you assess the near-term usefulness of virtual cell models?

items.question: How do you understand the Scottish proverb “Be happy when you're alive, for you're a long time dead” in relation to doing demanding research?
items.object: A Scottish proverb about happiness and its relevance to scientific research
items.answer: There's a Scottish proverb that I'm gonna butcher when I paraphrase, but it's basically, “Be happy when you're alive, for you're a long time dead.” That's real. I think that really hit for me when I read it. It was one of those, you're lying on the couch, the phone is six inches from your face, just beaming lux into your eyeballs right before you're supposed to fall asleep. I don't know, it reminded me that despite all the complexity of trying to work really hard to do useful things, you're supposed to have fun. I think we need more of that in life, not just in research labs, where it can be so easy to be super critical because that's the training and how you make progress is to hate on everything and everything has a problem and figure out why this can go wrong. Being optimistic and happy is not a path to mediocrity and mistakes, but it's actually how you have the emotional capacity for persistence over time to reach those long-term goals.
